speechtext:
Before the orders of the day are called, with the indulgence of the house I should like to direot attention to a rule which appears in Bourinot with regard to proceedings of this house. During the

debate on the address very wide latitude was allowed in regard to the practice of reading from prepared speeches. May I direct the attention of hon. members to the following passage in Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure, fourth edition, at page 335:
It is a rule in both houses of parliament that a member must address the house orally, and not read from a written, previously prepared speech; for the reason, that "if the practice of reading written speeches should prevail, members might read speeches that were written by other people, and the time of the house be taken up in considering the arguments of persons who were not deserving of their attention." It is the invariable practice to discountenance all such written speeches, and it is the duty of the Speaker to interfere when his attention is directed to the fact. Members may, however, make use of notes in delivering a speech.
I hope it will meet with the approval of the house if that rule is more strictly adhered to during the debate on the budget and in future debates in this house.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Following your general warning, Mr. Speaker, with respect to the reading of speeches, I shall endeavour to keep as far away from my notes as possible without getting lost. I may, however, have to refer to them occasionally in order to keep the trend of the discussion in some sort of respectable order before this honourable house.
May I at the outset extend my congratulations to the Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. Bennett) on his presentation to the house of one of the most comprehensive budgets delivered in Canada since the national policy was brought down in 1879. I am fortified in this view by expressions from one end of the dominion to the other by leading newspapers as well as by business men and others versed in this country's affairs. I desire to thank the Prime Minister on behalf of the people of Nova Scotia for the consideration extended to the coal-steel industry under the tariff readjustments and rail subventions. We have every reason to hope that they will be of inestimable value to the province down by the sea, and I feel I am expressing the unanimous sentiment of all those of independent thought in that part of the dominion when I say that the Prime Minister of the country has made an honest, sincere and, I think, most tangible effort to fulfil a pledge made by him to inaugurate in this country a national fuel-steel policy.
The budget may not be unanimously popular in the Dominion of Canada; that Was not the intention: it was not created for that purpose. A campaign budget was delivered in this house by the Hon. Mr. Dunning a little over a year ago. It was not a budget in the real sense as we understand them. This budget now before us is a business statement; it is not a campaign document. We are dealing at the present time not with theories but with conditions. The Dunning budget of 1930 dealt with theories and not with conditions. It lessened taxation when there was no justification in the world for doing so; and the Liberal party thereby conveyed to
2332	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Smith (Cumberland)
the people of Canada, with respect to the fiscal and financial affairs of this dominion, an impression which I am afraid misled them as to what that party intended to do in the future in matters of finance and trade. The people were expected to swallow all that was contained in the Dunning budget of 1930. But it occurs to me that the people thought they had their swallowing apparatus somewhat overtaxed and overworked during the past nine or ten years, swallowing doctrines contained in budgets and other pronouncements made by the King administration. On July 28 last, therefore, the people very wisely decided that they would no longer disturb their political digestion by swallowing a budget which was politically indigestible.
Considering the very thorough and capable manner in which the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) dealt with and disposed of the observations and criticisms made by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston), whom I am very sorry indeed I do not see in his seat at the present time, inasmuch as I should like to make some references to his statements, I do not deem it necessary-in fact, I think it would be useless-to traverse a great deal of the ground covered so admirably by the minister in his splendid and vigorous speech. But it will be my endeavour to confine myself to a few observations concerning tariff readjustments in their relation to coal and the rail subventions.
I said I regretted the fact that the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth was not present. He is a distinguished son of the province of Nova Scotia and I may say frankly that in common with his fellow-townsmen-* we both belong to the same place-I hold him in the highest esteem. I wanted to tell him that in my judgment he made a capable presentation, from his point of view, of this outstanding budget, but I cannot agree with his reasoning. The hon. member, in a speech lasting two hours, gave to the people of Nova Scotia but a scant ten minutes when he referred to the proposals contained in the budget which are bound to have a beneficial result to that province. He did not mention at all the steel industry, and referred only in a glancing way to the aid given to coal which is of such vital concern to the people of Nova Scoit-ia. The hon. member was very pessimistic over the budget, and considering the benefits we hope to result from the tariff readjustments and the rail subventions, it seems to me he was most unduly gloomy. The Liberals in that province are also most pessimistic; natur-< ally they are not pleased with some of the 
measures contained in the budget with respect to these important industries. It is natural to expect that they all would foe disturbed but I think the hon. member for Yarmouth should have said: Let us give these readjustments and subventions a fair trial. However, he was not willing to dio that but intimated that he did not expect there would be a change of any consequence in the quantity of coal placed in upper Canada or anywhere else through the provisions contained in the budget.
For the past number of years the newspapers mouthpiece of the Liberal .party in the province of Nova Scotia, located at Halifax, has been arguing with itself and a number of its fictitious readers that no government of the Dominion of Canada would have the courage to place an additional duty on coal because of the fact that other more thickly populated portions of the dominion were opposed to an increase in the tariff. During the last three campaigns in which I have been engaged, that was the main point argued against my reelection and against the attitude of the Conservative party. Although it W'as admitted that this party was protectionist and favoured safeguarding to some portions of Canada it was said that the protection promised would not be afforded to the coal industry because no government would have the courage to adopt such measures. Well, we have found a government that has had the courage to do it, and I think it has been done in a splendid-manner.
Not so many years ago a very prominent journalist in the province of Nova Scotia pamphleteered the entire country with a statement from his own pen that he was in faVour of regional tariffs because we had no hope whatever of obtaining tariff increases from any political party. It only goes to show that the Conservative party is standing true to its colours; it is a protectionist party and when it says it will do a thing, it does it.
There were some of us in the province of Nova Scotia, members of the Conservative party, and also a number of others-I might mention in particular the Halifax Herald which has been in the vanguard of every movement for the benefit of the maritime provinces-who had consistently maintained that if given the opportunity to legislate the Conservative party would place these vital basic industries in a position where they would be legitimately protected. Under the present budget and the readjustments which have been made in the tariff I think we might reasonably expect to reach an extended regional area in eastern Ontario and place there the products of the Nova Scotia mines to a degree which

The Budget-Mr. Smith (Cumberland)
we were not capable of doing before. If we were able to place upwards of a half million tons of coal in certain regions in the province of Ontario under the old subvention of one-fifth of a cent per ton mile surely an increase to one-third of a cent per ton mile will make it possible to extend that area that much farther west into Ontario. With the tariff increase on bituminous coal from fifty to seventy-five cents per ton, it is surely reasonable to expect that we will be able to penetrate farther into the Ontario region before we come in competition with the American coal which under the old rate overtook us before we got very far.
As I said before, this budget should be given a trial before being condemned. Yesterday the hon. member for Yarmouth said that he did not want to look a gift horse in the mouth; he is not only refusing to look a gift horse in the mouth but he is giving it the boot without inspecting it at all. I maintain that is not the view which should be taken in this important matter by an ex-minister of the crown coming from the province of Nova Scotia.
The decisions as to whether or not this budget will be ,of benefit to the coal industry of Nova Scotia need not be based upon what the hon. member for Yarmouth has said, or upon what any hon. member of this house might say; naturally our views are somewhat coloured, but I can give to the house views which are not coloured and which I think will prove to be convincing that what is contained in the budget is of great consequence to us. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one who is no longer young in point of years but is young in respect of membership in this house, I want first of all to congratulate .the rigiht hon. the Minister of Finance (Mr. Bennett) upon the remarkable speech made by him in this house on Monday. Especially do I wish to express my appreciation of the care he took to explain in the clearest of terms the financial structure of this dominion. I am sure his explanation of our financial status has proved as interesting to other new members as it did to me. Having rendered that tribute to his monumental! effort, however. I regret that now I have to express disappointment in the fact tthat his speech so clearly revealed that he is still unshaken in his faith in the efficacy of a high tariff policy as a tonic calculated to restore prosperity in Canada. So much has happened since the special session of 1930 which might have caused the right hon. gentleman to change his views on this subject I *had hoped that he would not only refrain from further increases in duties but might have been led even to reduce the duties which have been imposed on goods which might be brought in from Great Britain and her sister nations. I firmly believe that in the commonwealth of nations composing the great British Empire we will at all times find our best customers.
I want briefly to refer to some of the events to which I have alluded, events which in my opinion might have induced the Prime Minister to change his views. First of all I would refer to the reception tendered to the proposition he voiced at the Imperial conference in Great Britain. I think he himself would admit that his proposals were not favourably received. In this connection I would like to read to the house two comments on speeches made by British parliamentarians and recorded in the Journal of the Parliaments of the Empire for the. month of January,. 1931. At page 27 of that journal I find the following comments on the remarks by the Right Hon. J. H. Thomas:
Continuing, Mr. Thomas examined Mr. Bennett's proposals and said that in exchange for 10 per cent on foodstuffs, British soft coal, now taxed at Is. 7Jd. per ton into Canada, would get a benefit of 5 cents per ton. Germany, the Argentine, the United States and the Netherlands all admitted British coal free now'. Railway rails had a duty in Australia of 2s. and 4d. per hundredweight against Great

Britain - the Netherlands and Argentine admitted them free. Sew'ing machines had a preferential rate into Australia of 15 per cent against Great Britain, while Germany only imposed 9 per cent. Cotton goods-55 per cent in Australia, Canada 15 per cent, Germany 6 per cent, France 10 per cent, Netherlands and Argentine free. After quoting other percentages, Mr. Thomas asked whether there was any business man who would dare to take the risk of saying that it -would be a good proposition to accept the offer. It was only after the government had seen' exactly how it would work that they said: "No, it is not a good business proposition, and it cannot be accepted by us."
At page 37 of the same publication I find the following comment on the speech by the Right Hon. Philip Snowden:
It was said that the government had missed a great opportunity. They had missed the opportunity of taxing the food of the people, of adding to their economic burdens, of injuring a large part of their foreign trade. . . .
It did not take the government long to make up their minds and to come to a conclusion as to W'hat their attitude must be in regard to Mr. Bennett's proposal. It was the only proposal that was put before the conference from the dominions. The proposal was this:-"I am not going to reduce the tariff against the United Kingdom, but I will raise the tariff against the foreigner by 10 per cent of the present rate." That meant that if there were a duty of 30 per cent against the foreigner now, the duty would be raised to 33 per cent. Mr. Bennett had been returned to power a few weeks before it was necessary to come to the conference, and for a fortnight before he left Canada he was engaged in preparing for the conference by making large additions to the duties upon British imports into Canada.
His constituency was interested in woollen goods and had a large trade with Canada. The Canadian raised the duty upon 30-oz. woollen cloth from 7}d. to 2s.-3id. Scores of other instances could be given of similar action by Canada and Australia. Then Mr. Bennett came and said: "If you will put a tax upon foreign wheat, I am going to give you no reciprocity. I am going to keep the tariffs against the United Kingdom as they are."
I want to say at this point that I am absolutely in agreement with the views of many of the followers of the right hon. gentleman who attribute to him certain very admirable characteristics. Quite repeatedly I have heard hon. members on the other side of the house refer to the sincerity of the Prime Minister, to his courage, and to the bluntness and plainness of his speech. I agree he possesses these characteristics and because of them often I find myself admiring him. In particular, every time I hear him speak concerning matters of tariff I am more and more impressed with his sincerity. At the same time however I hope that my belief in his sincerity does not render it wrong of me to doubt his judgment. Certainly I am impressed with his courage; he is a very cour-

The Budget-Mr. Butcher
ageous man. He went to the Imperial conference in a most courageous spirit. However I am reminded of the old saying to the' effect that valour should be tempered with discretion. The fact is, however, that he is remarkably blunt, and I believe all hon. members to a certain extent admire bluntness. We do expect however that those who are blunt will tolerate bluntness in others.

speechtext:
Mr. Bennett has been
referred to as the outstanding man at the Imperial conference; no doubt that reference is correct. Mr. Snowden has said that Mr. Bennett was the only person who submitted a proposition to the conference; we find however that his proposals were not accepted by Great Britain. It seems to me that the right hon. gentleman holds the view that we can continue to sell to other countries without in turn buying from them. From his speeches I believe we may reasonably draw that inference. As a matter of fact, referring to the budget speech of the right hon. gentleman we find that he quoted with approval the remarks of the president of the United States Steel Corporation. The quotation is as follows:
It is a sound economic principle to sell in markets where the product is needed for consumption and where there is no surplus of the same commodity.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that that is very elementary economics. I wonder as a matter of fact that the president of the United States Steel Corporation would give expression to anything so elementary, and I certainly wonder that the right hon. gentleman saw fit to quote it. I think our manufacturers would say that to sell in any market whatsoever that will purchase our goods, not taking into consideration whether those goods are needed for consumption or whether there is a surplus of that commodity in the purchasing country, is a sound economic principle. I would go farther than that however and submit that even as an economic principle it is very imperfect. It is only fifty per cent of a principle, if I may say so, and there is a correlative fifty per cent which might be quoted as follows:	It is a sound
economic principle to buy only in markets that will buy from you your surplus products to at least approximately equal value. In other words, Mr. Speaker, I do not see how we can expect to find a market which needs our goods without purchasing something from that market in return. That is at least my personal conviction. We must bear in mind
also that we are not the only country that has surplus goods to sell, and if we will not buy from the countries which need the products we have to sell, they will find other countries which will buy their products.
I remember hearing an hon. gentleman say in this house some time ago that the present depression had existed1 in other parts of the world before it came into existence here. He said that after all we were in the backwash of that depression. I will go further and say that there has been over the world since the war a tariff mania. Would' it be incorrect, Mr. Speaker, to call it tariffobia? I think we might use that word. We find to-day that very many countries are regretting the stand they took in the past on this question. I said that one of the things which happened, which might have convinced the Prime Minister that it would be wise to amend his tariff policy, was the reception he received at the Imperial conference. I think a second matter might be the diminution of trade which is quite evident since the tariff policy of to-day came into force 'last September. A third point might be this: We find leading business men and economists throughout practically all the countries which have high tariffs beginning to move away from the idea that high tariffs are good for the country. We hear complaints on all sides, and I believe that in Europe, in parts of the United States, in Australia and in other countries associations of business men and economists are being formed with a view to inducing their governments to reduce tariffs.
Another reason was this: we expected a continuation of the Imperial conference in Canada this fall, and in view of what I would call the failure of the high tariff policy in the past I was hoping the Prime Minister might come to the house and say that no tariff increases would be made at this session, but that concessions would be made to other parts of the empire. At the same time the Prime Minister gave expression to that economic principle enunciated by the president of the United States Steel Corporation when he said:
May I point out to the house that all the domestic trade of this country which represents imports is foreign trade to some other country. . . . Our business is to see that we do not expand the foreign trade of any other country when we ourselves are producing or can produce the goods so imported.
Does that not apply to other countries also? Is it not true of every other country? That which may be exports from this country most certainly is imports to some other country, and other countries have as much right to

The Budget-Mr. Butcher

adopt those words and use them for themselves as we have. Then the Prime Minister said:
It is very simple.
Yes, I presume it is very simple. I will adopt those words as well, but I will go further and point out that I do not use the word "simple" with the same meaning. I looked in the dictionary before coming to the chamber to find the meaning of the word, and I find it has at least two meanings. The first meaning is "intelligible, clear, plain"; the second meaning is, "not wise or sagacious; silly." I would not for a moment say that any proposition brought .before the house by the Prime Minister is silly, but I do say that in my opinion it is not wise or sagacious to expect that we can continue to sell our surplus goods to other countries without buying anything in return.
I wonder if hon. members of this house have noticed how the spirit is spreading. Have you noticed that even the governments of our provinces are advertising that we should purchase the things we need only in our own province, and that we should not buy from other provinces if we can avoid it. Thus we have a "Buy in Saskatchewan" campaign and a "Buy in Manitoba" campaign, and it is worse than that. We find they are trying to put walls around our cities and towns. We are told that we should support home industries. That is all right; there is nothing wrong with that principle, but it can be amplified too much, in my opinion. There was one gentleman in western Canada who went even further than that; I refer to the Minister of Agriculture for Saskatchewan. According to the Manitoba Free Press of March 31 of this year:
. . . . Mr. Buckles also said that things that farmers used to make for themselves on the farms are now being made in factories, with the result that farmers now depend more and more on cash returns for their prosperity. "I have always maintained," the speaker said "that it should be the duty of every farmer to produce his own requirements."
So the farmer is to put a wall around his farm and manufacture what he needs himself and buy nothing outside; the town or city is to call upon its inhabitants not to deal with ether towns or cities; provinces are to call upon their people not to deal with other provinces, and the Dominion of Canada is to say, "We do not want to purchase from any other country." It is very simple indeed, I frankly admit.
The right hon. Prime Minister also made some statements with regard to inter-imperial trade. He said:
Hon. gentlemen opposite seem to find difficulty in working that out.

He was referring to the fact that there was no reason why we should not confine our trade largely to within the empire:
Of course they will find difficulty, for the simple and obvious reason that for nine years the colossal failures they made themselves indicate their inability to do so, and that is why we are here to-day.

speechtext:
Unfortunately I have no figures later than March 3ll, 1030. 'I was referring to the nine years to which the Prime Minister himself referred. The total trade increased from, roughly $1,501,000,000 in 1922, steadily every year until 1929, when there was a total trade of $2,654,000,000. Then it dropped in 1930, when it was $2,393,000,000. So that every year except last year there was an increase in the total trade done by the country. It seems to me, therefore, that the Prime Minister was not fair in stating that the Liberal party had been a colossal failure during the last nine years, so far as trade was concerned.
I shall now say a few words with regard to the Prime Minister's statement with reference to his proposed methods of raising revenue.

The Budget-Mr. Butcher
At page 2171 of Hansard the Prime Minister is reported as follows:
We propose, therefore, to indicate now to the house the methods to be adopted for the purpose of raising necessary revenue to meet expenditures. . . . Two principles have to be borne in mind; the first is that however tempting the field may be, in a period of great depression departure from known practised methods of taxation should be as slight as possible. In other words, there should be as little dislocation of business as possible and the taxes imposed should be those with which the people are familiar. The second is that taxes should be as light as possible having regard to the conditions which prevail.
I wish hon. members to note this:
Applying these rules first of all we take up customs duties, or the tariff. By this government the tariff is used for the purposes I have indicated. . . . With that in mind we have undertaken revision of only such items as it was necessary to deal with to ensure the maximum of employment by reason of the operation of the new rates. A similar result was obtained by our action during the last session.
It will be noted that the Prime Minister says that this is to be one of the methods employed for the raising of taxation. He says later that this was the idea in mind also in raising the tariff last session. The prime reason for doing this was to ensure employment in the country. It is quite clear, therefore, that his idea is that there shall be no imports of these particular goods. I ask, then: how can any revenue be raised, how will duties be imposed on goods that will not ibe imported-on goods in fact that cannot be imported, seeing that the reason for raising the tariff is to keep out such goods? The Prime Minister in this regard said:
I pause at this time to ask hon. members opposite what the condition of this country would have been had there been no short session. I just put that question to my hon. friends.
With his permission I will answer that question to the best of my ability. I say frankly that had there been no short session at all, and had no other arrangements been made to meet the serious conditions then prevailing, the results would have been disastrous to the country. I frankly admit that the expenditure of the $20,000,000, coupled with expenditures provided by the provinces, assisted very materially those who would otherwise have had no means of subsistence during the winter. But that is but one phase of the situation; there is another answer to the Prime Minister's question. Had there been no special session, but had the government instead, by governor general's warrant, allotted the sum of $20,000,000 for the purpose of relieving unemployment, the unemployment situation
22X10-149i
would have been relieved and, without that special session, we should not have had the increase in customs duties. And that, I believe, would have been all to the good of this country, for it would have enabled the Prime Minister to go to the Imperial conference in a very much better position to meet the situation that then existed than he was in view of the fact that we in Canada spent those two weeks raising the tariff against goods that might have been brought in from the old country.
The Prime Minister said further:
We, therefore, propose to provide that the freight rates shall be adjusted by this country absorbing 5 cents per bushel on all wheat that is exported of the crop of this year.
Now it is difficult even to comment on this statement inasmuch as the right hon. gentleman did not enlighten us how he proposed to see that this 5 cents should be paid. Personally I think there may be some difficulty. I do not say that the Prime Minister cannot get around it, but I do not for a moment see how wheat that is used for domestic purposes can be distinguished from wheat intended for export. When the wheat is sold by the load to the local elevator or is shipped by carload to the terminal elevator, it becomes a part of a very large bulk of wheat, and I do not see how you can distinguish the export from the domestic wheat. I suggest that a better way of doing it would be to have the 5 cents per bushel paid to the farmer when he delivers his load to the elevator, or added to his grain cheque when he receives payment. Then every farmer would receive that 5 cents.
Some hon. members, I understand, feel that it is not right for the farmers to be paid this 5 cents per bushel because it is a departure from the time-honoured principle which the farmers of the west at any rate have so long held, that there should be no bonuses to either farmers or industrialists. It does seem to me, however, that since the government has deemed it advisable to assist the manufacturers by imposing a duty on imported goods, and also to assure profits to corporations, the farmers are justified in accepting the 5 cents and wishing it were 10 instead.
With regard to the income tax, I wish the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) were in his seat, because I think he made a mistake in his speech yesterday. I do not think he intended to be misleading, but that is the effect of his words. At page 2312 of Hansard he is reported:
Let me state it clearly: the increase of 25 per cent in the corporation income tax will bear more heavily upon the richer men, and will cost them more than they would save by
[DOT]2340
The Budget-Mr. Coote

the reduction of the personal tax maximum to 25 per cent. Let us take the other point, the proposal in these resolutions to reduce to 25 per cent the maximum that may be taken in income tax. Why is that done?
I think the minister has made a mistake there, and the country will be very unwilling to accept the explanation he gave. Indeed, it seemed to me that he laboured very hard in making that explanation; he was not satisfied with it himself. As a matter of fact, I think you will find, if you look closely into the matter, that the man whose income is a million a year-there are not very many in Canada, but I understand there are some- will be taxed to the tune of $120,000 less than he would have been had the old income tax schedule remained in force.
I will close my remarks with one suggestion to the government. Notwithstanding all we may say, notwithstanding our unwillingness to advertise our troubles to the world at large, I firmly believe that the coming winter will see much of hardship and distress throughout the country as a result of unemployment and poor crops. It would be wise, therefore, for the government to prepare soon to provide for the needs of people who are suffering. In this country, with millions of bushels of -wheat to spare, with stares full of clothing, and with an abundance of fuel, it will be a .crime if our people are allowed to be hungry, Ill-dad or cold during the coming winter.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) took two and a half hours to deliver the budget speech which we are now considering, but as I am allowed only forty minutes I am sure the house will not expect me to cover the budget in detail. Like every budget which has been presented, there are some things in this one of which we approve and other things of which we disapprove. We will have to wait until the schedules are being considered in committee in order to have a complete discussion of these different proposals. However, there is one outstanding thing in this budget, the great deficit shown in the country's financial statement, the greatest in any year since I have had the honour to be a member of this house. I think one of the first things we should do is to inquire as to the cause of this deficit, amounting to something in excess of $75,000,000. A budget always gives some indication of the financial condition of the people. The revenues of this country are derived very largely from taxes on trade and if our revenue falls off it is a good indication that trade has also fallen off. One of the outstanding features of the Prime Minister's

statement is his attempt to balance the budget by means of drastic increases in taxation, on the one hand, and reduced expenditures, on the other. I do not think the budget can be balanced by such methods. It is a very fine thing to have the budget balanced but it is not essential. The Prime Minister does not occupy his present position because he promised the people to balance the budget; he is Prime Minister because he promised to cure unemployment, and I cannot find any suggestion in this budget that unemployment is to be cured. I do not think the budget as brought down will even reduce unemployment, and it does not hold out any *promise that unemployment relief will be granted to get us through this winter. The Prime Minister prided himself that this was a real budget, that he had given an estimate of the expenditures and revenues for the coming year, but so far as I am aware it does not contain any estimate of expenditure for unemployment relief this coming year. I trust that that is an oversight on the part of the Prime Minister because some provision must be made before this house prorogues to take care of the unemployed this winter. In my opinion this budget will not reduce unemployment. The only hope held out in this regard is that the tariff increases will bring about the establishment of more factories in Canada which will give employment to our people. What is the use of building more factories if we cannot buy back from the factories which we now have the goods which they can produce? What is the use of building more factories unless the people of Canada have money in their pockets, or credit in the bank wherewith they can buy the products of those factories? A lot of empty factories established through-out Canada will not do us any good.
If we are to continue under the capitalistic system it is absolutely necessary that we have some reform in our monetary system, and any budget which does not promise some such reform at a time like this I can class only as a failure-a failure to recognize conditions which actually exist. The proper way to secure a balanced budget is to increase the trade of this country, and then the taxes already levied will bring in sufficient revenue to balance the budget. Let me quote the Right Hon. Reginald McKenna, a prominent banker of London and a former Chancellor of the Exchequer. In referring to this question, he said:
Someone else may urge you to reduce the amount of money and bring down prices to the pre-war level or to such other arbitrary level as he happens to think the right one. Yes,

The Budget-Mr. Coote
and trade will remain depressed and the unemployed will be with you all the time. Moreover the burden of the national debt with the higher value of money will become intolerable, and no chancellor of the exchequer will be able to balance his budget.
There you 'have the case iput in a nutshell, and Mr. Reginald McKenna should be regarded as an authority on this question because of his experience as Chancellor of the Exchequer.
It is unfair to the people to increase taxation at this time, particularly to increase the sales tax. I cannot think of any words which Your Honour would regard as being parliamentary which would permit my expressing my opinion of the changes which have been made in the income tax in order to relieve some of those paying on large incomes. We will have to leave that matter until the bill itself comes down, but the change in the income tax and the increase in the sales tax bring to my mind a verse in the scriptures reading as follows:
For whosoever hath, to him shall be given; and whosoever hath not, from him shall be taken even that which he seemeth to have.
The cause of the present depression is the low price level of commodities, and particularly of the products of the farm. In an article appearing in the Sherbrooke Record of February 28, Mr. R. S. White, an hon. member of this house, writes as follows:
The aggregate value of all field crops produced in Canada in 1930 was $631,593,000 as compared with $948,981,000 in 1929, and $1,125,003,000 in 1928. That represents a tremendous shrinkage in the income of our farmers from- field crops, almost $500,000,000 in two years.
Is it any wonder trade and industry have declined in face of this immense reduction in farmers' income?
During -the last twelve months the prices of western grains have fallen 60 per cent; the prices of prime steers, 40 per cent and the prices of select hogs, 43 per cent. No other industry could stand such a cut in the prices of their products and the only reason why the farmer is carrying on to-day is because he is working without wages. The farmer is particularly hard hit because he sells at wholesale prices and buys at retail. The Bank of Nova Scotia, in their letter of March 31, state that since September, 1929, -the index of prices of Canadian farm products has fallen 46 per cent and of manufactured goods, 15J per cent while the index of retail prices has fallen only eight per cent. In other words, retail prices have fallen half as fast as wholesale prices, and only one-quarter as fast as -the price of farm products. Is it any wonder the farmer is not able to buy the products of our manufacturers?
The farmer suffers from still another handicap; he buys at Canadian prices, which are protected or inflated, and he sells at the prices prevailing on the open markets of the world.
I quote Mr. J. C. Armer, vice president of the Dominion Forge & Stamping Company, in support of my statement that Canadian prices are inflated, as follows:
Canadians pay more for their automobiles . than Americans pay for theirs. Canadians also pay more for all other manufactured articles than the selling price in some other parts of the world. They do this because it is the only way in which to build up a well-balanced nation which can provide work for all classes. Few people in Canada, however, realize that this price differential in motor cars is less than in most other manufactured articles.
I would direct the attention of the house to that last sentence. It is no wonder that the farmers of western Canada who have produced all these billions of new wealth which the Prime Minister talks about are now in their present condition. A five-cent bonus on the freight rate on wheat has been promised, and I suppose this is one of the compensating adjustments which the Prime Minister mentioned during the last campaign. This is the sugar coating on the protective tariff pill which the farmer must swallow. The coating is very thin but I suppose if the farmer has to swallow this pill it is just as well to have a little sugar coating. I regret the coating is not a little thicker; five cents per bushel is pretty small but I am glad that even that much has been granted. It looks as though the Prime Minister is having a little change of heart.
Over-production is blamed by the majority of people for the present depression, but I intend to try to make it plain that overproduction is not the cause of the present low price ievel. The Right Hon. Arthur Meighen said recently that he doubted whether there would be any over-production if the people could exchange their surplus products, one with the other. I think I am correctly interpreting his remarks. He also said:
The standard of living has increased and will continue to increase in proportion to the increased production provided the world's monetary system is such as to enable the exchange of those goods to be effective.
Mr. Meighen has put his finger on the weak spot in our economic system, that is the medium of exchange. Money was invented as the medium of exchange and let us consider that money includes the amount of bank credit which is in existence. We must look for the remedy in the whole monetary system. Professor Warren of Cornell university says:
The Budget-Mr. Coote

Prices are a ratio of the value of gold to the value of another commodity.
To assume that all commodities are overproduced and only gold is stable is like bringing the mountain to Mohammed.
But the majority of people in this and other countries appear to think the mountain should be brought to Mohammed. May I now quote Lord D'Abernon, a prominent banker in England who has often been quoted of late. In an address which he gave to the Royal Empire Society in London, England, recently, he said:
What had really occurred-without deliberate intention-was a hold-up in currency-
When anyone holds up a bank and we catch him, we put him into the penitentiary for a while, but the bankers hold up the entire country and nothing is done about it.

The falling currency has, it is true, brought apparent prosperity to German industry by means of a premium on exports,-
I want to emphasize these last words:
-which at the same time cripples the industries of competing countries.
Our wheat industry in Canada is being crippled by the competition of the Argentine and Australia because they have this 30 per cent advantage over us. What are we going to do about it? With a government pledged to protect the interests of the farmer I think that they should give us some depreciation to put us on an equal footing with our competitors and give us at least a fair chance. The only logical thing to do is to adopt the same measures which Australia and the Argentine have adopted and abandon the gold standard and allow our currency to depreciate. If any hon. members think I am exaggerating the beneficial effects of a depreciated currency, I would refer them to the speech of the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce, to which I have just referred, in June, 1922. I would quote further from it if I had time, but this forty-minute rule, as a friend of mine says, certainly cramps one's style.
I have here a report of the tariff committee of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, made in 1926. Four pages of it are devoted to this question of depreciated currencies showing how depreciation of the currencies of some European countries enabled them to undersell their competitors. May I quote just two sentences from that report? It says:
The depreciation in value of Belgian currency has resulted in large foreign markets being opened up for Belgian goods.
May I change the word "Belgian" to "Canadian", to show what would happen if we had our currency depreciated. It would then read thus:
The depreciation in value of Canadian currency has resulted in large foreign markets being opened up for Canadian goods.
I would like to make one further quotation from that report:
The Belgian manufacturer, favoured by the higher internal purchasing power of the franc, is enabled, owing to his lower cost of production, successfully to compete w'ith the British manufacturer.
I would like to change the word "Belgian" to "Canadian" and read it thus:
The Canadian manufacturer, favoured by the higher internal purchasing power of the dollar, is enabled, owing to his lower cost of production, successfully to compete with the British manufacturer.
I am absolutely convinced, Mr. Speaker, that if the present government had abandoned

the gold standard last September and had allowed our dollar to depreciate to the extent to which Australian and Argentine currencies had depreciated, it would have done more for t'he Canadian manufacturers than all the tariff increases introduced last September together with those contained in the present budget. There is absolutely no doubt about it.
Coming back to the farmers, I want to say that they are in an impossible position. Those who have money, and there are a few of them with a little money left, are producing at a loss. They are using up the capital they have built up over a long period of years, and it will be only a few years before they will be in the same position as those who are now bankrupt. What a shame that Canada should allow our farmers to get into that position! We have the most drastic legislation on the statute books of Canada, passed last September, to prevent the dumping of any goods into this country, and yet every bushel of wheat that we produce is being sold at dump prices whether it is sold in this country or elsewhere. What is being done about it? Canada has a very large export trade, and general business conditions are dependent on the prioe that we get for our exports. A depreciation of 20 per cent in our currency would increase the price of wheat 15 cents a bushel. I made that statement in a speech I made in the house some time agio, and in reading Hansard I noticed that the Prime Minister interjected, although I did not hear him at the time, "Surely the hon. member does not mean that." If I had heard him make that statement, I most certainly would have told him thalt I did mean it, and the statement is easily proved. When the price of wheat in Montreal is over 70 cents a bushel, if you allow the currency to depreciate 20 per cent, that will add 15 cents a bushel to the price of wheat; and if you allow the currency to depreciate by 30 per cent, as it has done in the Argentine, it will add 20 cents a bushel to the price of wheat, and that would enable our farmers to carry on, for 20 cents may be the difference between producing at a profit or at a loss.
The pulp and paper industry also needs help very badly. A depreciation in our currency of 30 per cent would put that industry back on its feet and would enable some of the companies .engaged in it to pay the interest on their bonds. It would increase the price not only of wheat but of all other grains, and of cattle and other farm products. It would increase the price of lumber, nickel, copper, zinc and coal. It would do more, in fact, to increase the returns to the coal indus-

The Budget-Mr. Coote
try, and would better enable the Canadian coal industry to secure the central Canada market than all the money the government proposes to spend under this proposed new fuel policy. I am not objecting to that fuel policy at all. I am glad to see that the government have at last brought down a fuel policy. I am sorry that I have not time to deal with that subject to-day. By depreciating our currency the price of all our exports would be increased just to the extent of whatever depreciation took place. It would probably mean a difference to us of anywhere between $250,000,000 and $300,000,000 per annum. This increased amount of money put into circulation would do more to stimulate business in Canada and create employment than any other thing which this government could do right at the moment. It would restore some of the confidence which is now so sadly lacking. If the currency did not depreciate fast enough, and some people tell me that it would not, we could easily arrange that by a little inflation. There are a lot of people who think that if you label anything as inflation you have at once discredited it. Unfortunately there is that impression, but in that connection let me read what Professor Soddy of England has to say in regard to it:
Whereas no changes of revenue, so long as the currency remains constant, affect the relative proportion of the whole revenue secured by the creditors, any increase of currency diminishes their relative share and hence is known as inflation, while any decrease increases their relative share, and hence is called sound finance.
We certainly have the sound finance just now, but it is very disadvantageous to our people. A little measure of inflation would easily be justified. Professor Day, of McGill university, in a speech reported in the Montreal Gazette of February 28 last, says, although to be fair to Professor Day I must add that he did not suggest the abandonment of the gold standard:
A reasonable general inflation might easily be justified now as merely correcting the excessive deflation of values which is giving us so much trouble.
Mr. Neill, in his statement to the annual meeting of the Royal Bank expressed somewhat the same opinion. Speaking of the restoration of the previous stabilized price level, he says:
To accomplish this, money must again flow freely through the financial arteries of the world.
We cannot regulate this matter for the world, but we could arrange that money should flow more freely through the financial arteries of Canada. This can only be done
if we suspend redemption of our notes in gold. Under the present system we can put more money out, but it will not stay out. It will come back for gold. It might be advisable to stabilize the dollar at 70 or 75 cents. I am not going to say just where the dollar should be stabilized. If it is to be stabilized the main factor to be used in determining the point at which this should be done would be the cost of living in Canada. To allay the fears of those people who think the cost of living would increase in proportion to the depreciation which would take place may I quote the words of Professor Plumptre:
If we raised the price of gold one-fifth, and the exchange is moved against us to that extent, all our imports would cost us that much more. The cost of living would be raised slightly (Not more, probably than 3 to 4 per cent since the cost of imports at wholesale constitutes but a small proportion of the cost of living). This arbitrary raising of the cost of living, might, in more normal times, have been called an injustice, but after the year 1930, in which wholesale prices have fallen about 20 per cent and retail about 8 per cent, a plan which attempts to restore them towards their 1929 level can hardly be called unjust. It might be called inflation, but the proper term would be anti-deflation.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure no harm will be done to anybody if the cost of living does not rise beyond the point it reached in 1926. According to the words of Professor Plumptre, we could have a depreciation of 30 per cent without reaching the 1926 level. Some people who object to the suspension of the gold standard say that if we abandon it we can never get back to it again. Those people remind me of the old lady who watched the operation of Stephenson's steam engine. She watched the locomotive get up steam and volunteered the remark "that thing will never run." However it did run, and she said, throwing up her hands in terror, "My God, it will never stop!"
We abandoned the gold standard in 1914 and our dollar came back to par in 1923. We went back to the gold standard in 1926. I wonder why we fear abandonment at the present time? When lately a banker expressed this fear to me I said, " There has not been a time since confederation when the bankers could not get the government to do anything they wanted. Why do they fear that in the period ahead of us, in the days that are to come they will not be able to go to the government, when the proper time comes and say that the time has arrived to return to the gold standard?" I know probably some of the bankers would object, but that is no reason why we should not carry out the suspension.
The Budget-Mr. Coote

At this time I wish to quote the remarks of Professor Soddy:
Institute a complete organization for ascertaining, on every public proposal, the feeling of the city, and the views of the captains of finance and banking, but act in precisely the opposite direction. From the point of view of the welfare of the community rather than of its creditors, you could hardly fail to be right every time.
I think there is a great deal of truth in that paragraph. There are just one or two other points I wish to emphasize before my time has elapsed. One point I wish to 'bring to the attention of hon. members is that lower price levels increase debt. Surely the fact is apparent to anyone that if the prices of commodities produced in Canada are reduced a larger share of such commodities is required to pay interest and to pay debt. The debts of producers are stated in terms of dollars. When the producer has to pay more of his products for interest bills and for instalments on the principal of his debt he has that much less money left to purchase the product of the factories in Canada. That is one of the reasons we have so much unemployment today. The bonded debt 'of Canada including dominion, provinces and municipalities is approximately four and a quarter billion dollars, not taking into account the debt of the Canadian National Railways. There are no figures available as to the amount of private debts, but it is safe to assume that they are greater than the public debts. I heard a man estimate recently that the total debts in Canada would certainly be in excess of ten billion dollars, or at least one thousand dollars per capita for our total population, including men, women and children. The burden on our people of that debt is so tremendous that we cannot afford to allow it to be increased. The interest on such debts can be paid only out of production. Sir Thomas White is reported to have said that if Canada's war debt were ever to be repaid it would be from the top six inches of 'Canada's soil. Our present monetary policy is making production impossible. The debts of the western farmer have been doubled iby the low price level of farm products. Pretty soon he will be unable to produce. When he finds himself in that position I wonder how the interest on our debts will 'be paid. The same is true of our pulp and paper industry. If the debts of that industry are to be repaid the price of the commodity that industry is producing must be raised.
At this time, Mr. Speaker, I have come to a statement which I hesitate to make. I feel compelled to say however that unless some action is taken to improve prices of staple

farm products and other commodities, we are faced with business stagnation and human suffering beyond my power to describe. The prospects are that hundreds of schools will have to be closed and thousands of farmers will be forced into bankruptcy. School and municipal debentures will have to be defaulted; millions of dollars invested bv loan, trust and life insurance companies in farm mortgages and millions of dollars of bank loans will have to be written off. Our whole financial structure is endangered. Thousands of people of moderate means living on rents and interests will find their incomes wiped out and thousands of our people will be thrown out of employment, thousands of lives will be sacrificed. What for? Aparently all this havoc is to be wrought merely to maintain the gold standard. I think the statement made by the late William Jennings Bryan, that the people are being crucified on a cross of gold is certainly coming true to-day. Why should we be afraid to consider depreciation? Why should we be afraid to abandon the gold standard? We did it in 1914, and the situation with which we are now confronted is just as serious as the situation which confronted parliament at ithat time. Why can we not suspend our gold standard at this time?
I admit-and with these words I will close my remarks-that this depreciation would not be a solution for all the economic problems facing us now. Beyond a doubt however such depreciation would increase the purchasing power of those engaged in agriculture, in our forests, in our mines and fisheries, and' enable them to buy more shoes, clothes, furniture, automobiles, radios and other products of our manufacturing industries. This depreciation would do more to increase employment in the industries I have mentioned than all the changes this budget will make in the tariff. It will d'o more than anything, else to solve the problem facing the Canadian National Railways. It will enable the Minister of Finance to balance the budget without the drastic increase in taxation which he now proposes. In the meantime we should endeavour to arrange a conference of world powers to discuss the proposal of Mr. Darling to monetize silver. We should adopt the suggestion of the bon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) to establish in Canada a bureau of economic research. We should procure the best brains available in Canada and charge them with the task of suggesting an economic system which will enable us to distribute among our own people, not only all the food, clothing and shelter they need but also some of the modern conveniences which we can produce so well.

The Budget-Mr. Hackett
Mr. JOHN T. HACKETT (Stanstead): Mr. Speaker, in the short time at my disposal I wish to discuss only one topic, that of the growing debt of the Canadian National Rail" ways. First I shall speak of the period which has elapsed since the beginning of 1923. Since that time the funded debt of the Canadian National Railways has been increased by $433,010,171 and the unfunded debt by 88,993,000, making a total of $442,003,171. There has been advanced to the Canadian National Railways in the same period, in cash and by appropriation, the sum of $101,056,396.15, making a total of $543,059,567.96. During the same period the funded debt to the public has increased from $823,099,056 to $1,238,565,862. and the interest owing and annually paid to the public on this funded debt has increased from $34,652,324.38 during 1922 to slightly over $54,000,000 in the current year. I would warn those who take the trouble to check my figures to beware of the hiatus of three months between the close of the railway year, which ends with the calendar year, and the close of the departmental year, which ends on the 31st March. The figures I have given are for the period ending March 31 last.
So much for the period from 1923 to 1931. There is another period beginning in 1909 and another item of $604,406,239.42 which was the subject of some discussion between the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston), who replied to the budget speech. I find that the item was paid in its entirety to the constituent companies of the Canadian National Railways, and to the Canadian National Railways, between the years 1909 and 1923. After consolidation of these constituent companies in 1923 the Canadian National received $57,482,652 of this amount. It is well to recall that these figures refer exclusively to the Canadian National Railways and the companies which constitute it, exclusive of what we call government lines, which include the old Intercolonial railway, the line in Prince Edward Island, the National transcontinental and the Hudson Bay railway. This amount of $604,406,239.42, less about $156,329,236, was paid to the constituent lines which go to make up the Canadian National Railways, after 1919. Why interest should not be paid on these amounts; why they should be called bookkeeping entries and consequently not debts payable is a matter concerning which I will require additional information. At the moment I cannot see why these amounts should be treated otherwise than as money loaned upon which interest should be paid.
Now let us turn for a moment to the report of the Canadian National Railway System for
the year 1930. We find that its liabilities amount to $2,919,000,000. At this point I should like to ask why such an unusual and misleading system of accountancy has been adopted in this report. The liabilities amount to $2,919,000,000; the deficit amounts to $575000,000, yet the total given at the bottom of the column on page 15 is $2,344,000,000. If the ordinary rules of accountancy were observed we would have a total of $2,919,000,000 on the side of the liabilities and a red ink entry on the side of the assets showing a deficiency of $575,000,000, I point this out, Mr. Speaker, because I think it imperative that the people of this country should foe afforded every facility to know more accurately than they do know the exact situation of this, vast transportation system which we are attempting to administer and which has made such terrible drains upon our resources.
In going over these liabilities we find that the railway company has been called upon to pay interest, or has paid interest, only on one item going to make up the total $2,919,000,000. It has paid interest on the funded debt owing to the public, which amounts to $1,168,000.000. It has charged itself with but has not paid $32,067,462.53 interest on the loans from the Dominion of Canada, amounting to $604,000,000. On the balance of over a billion dollars owing to the dominion it has paid no interest and has not charged itself with any. Therefore I submit that the argument in favour of eliminating from the computation the ordinary interest charges upon the $604,000,000 is without cogency or point. Despite the fact that we have put into this system some $543,000,000 of new capital, it has gone on accumulating deficits from year to year. In round figures those deficits were:
1923		 $51,697,000
1924		 54,860.000
1925		 41,444.000
1926		 29,894,000
1927		 37,636.000
1928		 33,350,000
1929		 40,933.000
1930		 61,287,000
With regard to the years 1928 and 1929 I have not stated the full deficit, because I have been unable to find the deficit on eastern lines, although I know it is substantial. During those eight years this system has accumulated deficits amounting to $351,000,000, an average of $43,888,162 per annum. If one were to comply with the suggestion made, that the interest on $604,000,000 be entirely eliminated, we should then have a total deficit over these eight years of more than $100,000,000, or an average deficit or more than $12,000,000 per annum. I think such a result is worthy of the thoughtful consideration of
The Budget-Mr. Hackett

the people at large and of the careful scrutiny of the house in particular. I told the house, when I spoke briefly on this subject a few weeks ago, that I considered the peril to our financial fabric, to our national credit and even to our solvency was both real and imminent as a result of the ownership of this system.

speechtext: What would the hon. gentleman suggest?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I am grateful to the
hon. member for the suggestion, because it affords me an opportunity to tell him that private ownership, of which he complains, has done more for Canada's credit and for the people of Canada than any system, of which this one under discussion may be the prototype, can ever do for the country. And if the hon. gentleman-I am sorry he has found it necessary to leave the chamber-will take the annual report of the Canadian Pacific Railway for last year, he will find that this road, which I daresay he would style a predatory institution, after paying 10 per cent, dividends and all its fixed charges, paid out but $4,000,000 more than the interest which the Canadian National pays annually on its funded debt to the public of Canada, overlooking entirely the $604,000,000, on which it pays nothing, and the other thousand million which it did not take into consideration at all.
I would tell the hon. gentleman that public ownership is incapable of bringing to the administration of business that prudence and skill which private ownership can furnish. And I would furthermore tell him, if he wishes to carry the point a step further, that so long as governments are what they are it is absolutely impossible to obtain efficient administration under government control, cloaked thinly as it may be by independent or so-called independent administration. If the hon. gentleman doubts me, I would ask him to

read any page of the history of Canada which refers to the railways. I would ask him to go back to the year 1903, when the government began to dabble in rather a big way in railways. I admit candidly that Canada has built railways for .reasons other than profit. It built the Intercolonial to fulfil a pledge; the Canadian Pacific Railway was built to fulfil another pledge. And it may be necessary to help these roads from time to time to overcome geographical difficulties and satisfy political exigencies. In the early years of this century, we had one privately-owned transcontinental road which was moderately prosperous and moderately efficient and which was satisfying the needs and requirements of our people. What happened? Mackenzie and Mann began to build roads on the prairies, and about 1903 they sought an o-utlet toward the Pacific and another toward the Atlantic. It was then that the Grand Trunk, becoming jealous, wished to construct a transcontinental road of its own. It was then that the Dominion government, headed by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, decided that the government would finance a transcontinental railway and would have a great deal to say with regard to its construction and something to say with regard to its administration and operation. I should like to tell the hon. gentleman who interrupted me, were he here, just how far we went astray, how far the parliament of Canada went astray, and how far that eloquent chieftain of the Liberal party was able to lead the people astray, when he engaged it in public ownership. I say, without disrespect to the memory of that great man, that if there be one blot upon his reputation as a man of affairs and a man of prescience, that blot lies in the fact that he engulfed this country in the abyss of public ownership of railways.
I turn back to the days of 1903 and I ask you to listen to the utterances of Sir Wilfrid Laurier with regard to the construction of this railway. When it was contended by the then Hon. Mr. Borden that it was not the time to construct another Transcontinental system, that the need was not imperative and that there was no necessity for it, Sir Wilfrid said, urging immediate construction:
. Such is our duty; it is immediate and imperative. It is not of to-morrow, but of this day, of this hour, and of this minute. Heaven grant that it be not already too late.
That was what Sir Wilfrid Laurier said in 1903. I will tell the house what he said about the cost of constructing the road. Hon. members will recall that the government of which Sir Wilfrid Laurier was leader undertook to build the National Transcontinental

The Budget-Mr. Hackett
from Winnipeg to Moncton and to pay the carrying charges on it until the Grand Trunk Pacific, which had undertaken to construct a road from Winnipeg to the Pacific with bonds guaranteed by the Canadian government- which it has since paid-was ready to operate both. The house will recall that Sir Wilfrid told the country and parliament that there would be practically no expense in connection with it. I would ask the house to take note of the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, which appear at page 7676 of Hansard of 1903, as follows:
Therefore, let our friends on the other side of the house, and let our friends on this side of the house also, take note of this fact, that with the exception of a few years of interest, to which 1 shall allude later on. we shall have this portion of the railway built by the government from Moncton to Winnipeg without the cost of one dollar to the Canadian people."
And again at page 7690:
Now, sir, what is the liability incurred by the government for the construction of this road from Winnipeg to the Pacific ocean?
And again:
-and the total interest for three years will be $3,780,000. This is the whole of the liability which is incurred by the government for the construction of the railway from Winnipeg to the Pacific ocean.
And then on page 7691:
The sum total of the money to be paid by the government for the construction of that line of railway from Moncton to the Pacific ocean will be in the neighbourhood of $12,000,000 or $13,000,000, and not a cent more. Now, sir, what is $13,000,000 in the year 1903?
In reply to tihe lion, gentleman who asked me what I thought of government ownership, I will say that the thirteen millions in the year of grace 1903 have rolled up until they represent the larger portion of a thousand millions of dollars to-day. It is largely be-oause the government of 1903, in the face of all the hazards, the difficulties and the perils which surround undertakings of this kind, made its noble experiment in public ownership, that the people of this country are labouring to-day under the heavy burden which was placed upon them by an administration of that time.
All of this may be somewhat irrelevant, because we have government ownership, we have got the Canadian National, or possibly it might be more accurate to say that the Canadian National has got us. All of which reminds me of an episode which occurred recently; two of the principals were known to me. These gentlemen were fishing on one of the lakes which stud the eastern townships. One of them espied something crossing the lake which investigation disclosed to be a
bear. The anchor rOpe was used as a lasso and the bear was caught. To the amazement of my friends the bear not only swam toward the boat but nearly upset it as he clambered in. One of the party said, "Now that we have got him, what are we going to do with him?" The other replied, "Now we have got him, what is he going to do with us?" This turned out to be a very pertinent remark, as the sequel shewed: bruin manned the ship and the fishermen sought sanctuary in the icy waters of the lake. I do not wish to push the analogy further.
I will now attempt to answer the question put to me by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) when he asked: What are we going to do with this system? I take it for granted that this country is incapable of bearing up under a burden of from $40,000,000 to $50,000,000 of deficits each year; I take it that this house is unanimous in the decision that such a condition cannot be allowed to continue. If it cannot go on, what are we to do?
At this point let me pause long enough to say that a by-product of this administration of the railways by the government has been the undoing or near undoing of another national institution. The Canadian Pacific Railway is an institution in which the people of this country and of other countries have invested large sums of money. It is a system of transportation which is known all over the world, not only on this continent but on the seven seas. Parliament has so conducted itself towards the administration of the Canadian National that it has placed a price on the head of the Canadian Pacific Railway; it has placed a bonus on the bankruptcy of that company and the day will come and come rapidly, unless something is done to curtail the rivalry between these two roads -parliament can curtail it because it is parliament which supplies the funds-when we will see the Canadian Pacific beaten to its knees. That company already has cut its dividends and the wages paid to its workers; its officers and men are now working three days a month without remuneration. If it passes its dividend entirely and becomes bankrupt it will then behoove this country to take it over and the government will then have a monopoly of transportation. If the government bring to bear upon that monopoly all the skill and wisdom which has characterized its administration of our national railways, we may then have a Pretorian guard but no emperor.
In reply to the question, "What are we going to do?" asked by the hon. member for North Winnipeg, I reply that we must
The Budget-Mr. Hackett

eliminate this annual deficit. The suggestion of writing off the liabilities is childish. It is no remedy. That was the method adopted by our friend of other days when bluebooks did not exist. Mr. Harold Skimpole refused to learn how to count so he would never know how much he owed. Thus he was always at peace with himself if not with his creditors. One way of making this system pay or making it cease to be a drain upon our resources is by raising the tolls. I can imagine how popular that action would be, especially in the land slightly beyond that represented by .my hon. friend from Winnipeg. Nevertheless, be it said that the freight rates in this country are from 10 to 15 per cent lower than they are anywhere else in the world, and also let it be said that the only portion of our railway system which .pays is that portion which lies in the United States where they have an adequate rate.
Another way is to reduce the wages and salaries of the men who operate the road. I know full well that that would create a terrible outcry. These wages and working rules were fixed by Mr. McAdoo some years ago when he was seeking a presidential nomination in the United States, and they have made a heavy demand ever since upon the earnings of all railway systems. Were wages decreased I know that many hon. members who sit in this house would disappear, that might not be the greatest calamity. Possibly I would be of the number as my constituency is traversed iby no less than three railway lines, and I am sure that the railway men do not desire that their wages and salaries be diminished. But the extent by which we shall have to raise tolls or diminish salaries and wages depends upon the extent to which we are able to make savings elsewhere. There are opportunities and methods which are apparent to all of effecting substantial saving alsewhere.
In the first place we are told that passenger traffic does not pay, yet we find the most lavish and competitive passenger traffic in the world operated by the Canadian National system. We are told in their magazine, which they publish monthly, that the finest, fastest, most luxurious and best equiped train in the world operates between Montreal, Toronto, Detroit and Chicago. We know there pull out of Ottawa many luxurious and fast trains each day for Toronto and Montreal. We know that ancillary to this passenger service there has been established on the Pacific coast a boat line-and heaven forbid at this junction that I make any reference to our merchant marine other than as an incident 
to the folly which I am now discussing. It has lost to Canada almost as much money in comparison with its size, age and opportunity as the Canadian National itself. We have on the Pacific a boat line which is losing money every trip that is made. We have put nearly 120,000,000 into hotels. I do not happen to come from Halifax, but I make bold to say that Halifax has about as much need for a Canadian National hotel as any small village in any constituency which is represented here might have for an hotel of equal cost. We also know a hotel was built in Charlottetown. We know that in Saskatoon they are spending $4,000,000 on a hotel. We know that a hotel is operated in Winnipeg. We know they are building a hotel in Vancouver, and the Canadian National magazine devotes pages to a description of it.
