speechtext:
What about the
Canadian Pacific?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
The great difference between the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific is that the Canadian Pacific hotels have paid and the Canadian National hotels have never paid and cannot pay. In the hotel here in Ottawa there has been installed a swimming pool which has cost from half a million to a million dollars. What possible return is there on it? The Canadian Pacific has its hotel at Banff and we have dropped' our millions into Jasper, for what purpose? We are told that the passenger service cannot pay; that it does not pay on any railway, and yet we are spending these vast sums without purpose or point or possibility of return. I read in this morning's paper that the' telephone system on the train running between Montreal and Toronto cost $83,333.21 last year and yielded monthly but $73.43. We have radios on all these trains. These things are insignificant in themselves but they point to a lavishness, a desire to spend on the part of the management which bodes ill for economy I pass to another opportunity to save after we have eliminated some of these luxuries. In Montreal we find at the present timd this longing to be lavish, to expand and to spend, seeking its final expression. I do not deny that the quarters into which the Canadian National now runs are entirely unseemly and unbecoming; I admit that better quarters should be provided, but what is required in Montreal is a union station. If the Canadian National station and the Canadian Pacific station were separated by ten miles, the solution would be very obvious and easy;.

Private Bills
everybody would see what was required and everybody would know what to do. But because they are but three or four hundred feet apart, we are told it is absolutely impossible to bring them together. It behooves parliament to see that a union station is built. Parliament is providing the money. A separate Canadian National station will bring in its wake a Canadian Pacific station, because the Canadian Pacific must follow suit or admit it is worsted, and not a penny's return will result from either venture! It is largely within the control of parliament to determine whether or not this great source of waste shall continue.
I now pass on to another source of waste, and that is the terminals that are being constructed in Montreal. We have heard a great deal about the Palmer report. Let me turn to it and read to the house the final paragraph of the 45th section:
As a whole, the service would be excellent, but worked in two separate and competitive interests, many of the advantages of adequate distribution are vitiated.
We find there that a new and unnecessary line of elevated railway is to be built about Mount Royal from Longue Point to Eastern Junction when there already exists such a line. The Canadian National, in order to bridge a gap on the water front of a little over a mile, is now running out to l'Epiphanie and back, a distance of 109 miles. It wishes to construct a line nine miles in length, when, if it were given running rights over a portion of the Canadian Pacific, it could save 85,000,000, cut off five miles of the distance which it would have to run over the line which is projected, and thus avail itself of an excellent opportunity of saving money which is so sadly needed for other purposes.
We have babbled much in the house about Russia and her five-year plan. We have marvelled at the blind enthusiasm which has held this people in its grasp while it went forth to accomplish most difficult and painful tasks. We have marvelled at the forbearance and docility of that people and of that country. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the blind and dumb docility of that people has found a perfect prototype in the docility and blindness of the Canadian people. Blindly we have followed the administration of this road, up not five, but nine years of vistaed hopes, and I for one refuse mutely to follow that administration further down into the vaulted gloom of financial dissolution. It is there that we are going unless some means can be found to stay this orgy of spending: and, Mr. Speaker, the danger is not all there. I do not wish to underestimate or understate the ability, energy and driving force of the man who, to use a colloquialism, has put the Canadian National on the map, but I do say that he has overshot the mark; he has gone too tar. The other night, speaking in the house, I ventured in terms courteous and with honesty of purpose to make some reference to the way in which this property is being administered. The next night in Winnipeg, the gentleman in question is reported to have made some reference to a certain long-eared animal that had so perfectly acquired the art of kicking that he became the author of his own undoing. In the press he is reported to have said, "Let those who attack us, hop to it." Mr. Speaker, if that was an invitation, it was entirely unnecessary. If it was a threat, it was entirely unworthy. That gentleman in charge of the administration of the Canadian National Railways-independent administration is a fiction as long as parliament supplies the funds; if we are honest we must admit it -is the servant of the people of Canada. He must accept orders from the parliament of Canada. If when criticized by parliament he resents that criticism in the tone in which he resented the honest and straight-forward criticism which was levelled at the company a few weeks ago, he has lost that sense of proportion necessary to a useful servant either of the road or of the country.

Mr. ANGUS MacINNIS (Vancouver South) moved the second reading of Bill No. 45, to amend the Canada Shipping Act.
Explain.

When the Marine estimates were under consideration a few days ago, there came up some items which had a bearing on this bill. In that discussion it was pointed out that the existing shipping act was passed in the year 1854, that is to say, thirteen years prior to confederation. The act as passed ait that time and as it now stands on the statute books has remained pretty much the same except for a few minor amendments. I am advised that no amendments whatever have been passed since that time, affecting common seamen, and the amendments now proposed are intended to improve the conditions under which such seamen work and to bring those conditions more into harmony with modern requirements. In 1913 the Minister of Marine of that day, the Hon. Mr. Hazen, prepared various amendments to the act and submitted them to the interested parties, with a view to a complete revision

Canada Shipping Act
of our shipping law. Owing to .the outbreak of the war, however, in 1914, that revision was abandoned. In 1923, and again- in 1924, the Trades and1 Labour Congress of Canada adopted a resolution with reference to the act, submitting a number of amendments. They declared:
Whereas the Canada Shipping Act as at present constituted is obsolete so far as its application to conditions of the day is concerned, and contains many weak clauses which give the operators of steamship lines a chance to evade the real intention of the act-
And they go on to ask f-or various amendments. These amendments -have been urged at every convention of the congress from 1923 to the present time. The first amendment proposed is section 213A, which applies to the physical examination of seamen, and the section as we have it here is taken from the Merchant Shipping Act of Great Britain, which has been in effect there since 1894. The section which we propose is slightly different from the British act so far as the last two lines are concerned:
And if such report finds that the seaman is not in a fit state for duty at sea, he shall not be employed.
These two lines do not appear in the British Shipping Act of 1894. The next amendment proposed is section 213B, which refers to the inspection of provisions and water intended for the use of the crew of any Canadian sea-going ship. At present there is no inspection of food or water on our ships. Any three members of the crew of a ship may make complaint in reference to provisions or water and an inspector is appointed to inspect such provisions and water and report back to the port officer. If, however, the complaint of these members of the crew is not substantiated by the inspection and it is found that neither the food nor the water is of inferior quality, the crew are penalized by the imposition of a fine amounting to a week's wages. I think the committee will agree that this is rather drastic. This proposed section provides:
"213B. (1) All provisions and water intended for the use of the crew in any Canadian seagoing ship shall be inspected either on board the ship or before shipment, and if on such inspection the provisions or water are found to be in any respect deficient in quality, the ship shall be detained until the defects are remedied. Such inspection shall be made within the three days before the ship proceeds to sea, and another inspection shall be made if the inspecting officer has reason to suspect that any of the articles inspected have been subsequently removed, injured or destroyed.
Subsection 2 of this section 2-13B, reads:
(2) If the inspecting officer is of opinion that the articles inspected are deficient in 22110-150
quantity or quality, or are placed in improper receptacles, he shall give notice in writing to the shipping master of the port where the ship is lying, and also to the master, owner or consignee thereof, and the master of the ship, before proceeding to sea, shall produce to the shipping master a certificate under the hand of the inspector that the defaults found to exist have been remedied, and if such certificate is not produced, the ship shall be detained until it is produced.
Subsection 3 provides for a scale of provisions for the use of Canadian registered ships, in accordance with the first schedule to the Merchant Shipping Act of 1906. A few days ago I read the schedule and 1 need not go into that phase of the matter to-night.	*
I submit that these provisions are very reasonable and I do not think there can be any real objection to them. The next section which we propose refers to the working hours of seamen on all Canadian sea-going ships. We are asking that they shall not exceed eight hours a day except in cases of emergency. My information is that not only do ordinary seamen work more than eight hours a day but that they are working as a rule seven days a week and do not get a day off except when they are discharged. This refers to ordinary seamen, firemen, trimmers and so forth. The eight hour day is fairly well recognized now as the ordinary working day in all trades, and with the extent of unemployment in Canada to-day I do not think there is any reason why any man should be asked to work more than eight hours. As a matter of fact, we cannot provide eight hours of work a day for a great many people in the dominion at the present time.
Subsection (2) of section 213C, which refers to compensation for injuries, reads as follows:
The master or owner of every such ship for which an agreement with the crew is required under this act shall make provision for the payment of compensation to any member of the crew suffering an injury arising out of his employment, equal to that paid under the Workmen's Compensation Act in the province in which the ship is registered.
The reason for drafting that subsection in -that way is because a doubt exists that the Dominion government has power by statute to bring any industry wi'thin the provisions of the provincial compensation acts, and this amendment places the onus in regard to an injured seaman upon the owner or -master of a ship. Under the present Canada Shipping Act the owner's obligation to the seaman ends when the seaman is brought into port, and in many cases these men are left stranded without any provision being made for convalescence. The

Canada Shipping Act

substance of this subsection was discussed some few days ago under a resolution introduced by the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Ross) and I understand that the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) agreed that this is possibly the best way to deal with the matter.
Subsection (1) of section 560 deals with a board of steamship inspection, and provides that a representative from the National Association of Marine Engineers shall be a member of this board. I think the principle has been fairly well established that in a matter of this kind where the employees are concerned, they should have representation.
Reverting again to the section dealing with compensation, I should like to refer to the manner in which the compensation act works in the province of British Columbia. Where a man is hired in a port in the province he is covered by the compensation aot, but should he be hired in a foreign port he does not receive these benefits. It is possible to have on the same ship members of the crew who are covered by the act and others who are not, and there is a tendency to discriminate in favour of seamen picked up at foreign ports, because in that case the owners would not be liable under the British Columbia compensation act for compensation in case of injury. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company have ships sailing from Vancouver to Australia, and the seaman taken on in Vancouver is covered by the aot but should a member of the crew be taken on in Australia he is not covered. That is a defect in the act which should be remedied.
The next section of the bill covers subsection (1) of section 935. When this bill was up for first reading the Prime Minister stated that possibly certain of the sections would be ultra vires of the dominion parlia-i ment. I believe this is the section to which he was referring, and I think ithe objection is well taken. I do not intend to say anything on this section or to press it, because I 'believe it to be ultra vires of this parliament.
The amendments asked for are quite simple, and unless there is some difficulty in administration I see no reason why they should nob pass at this time, regardless of the fact that the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) has stated that he contemplates a general revision) of the act in the near future. I do not know just how soon that revision will take place. It may be within a year or so, but in the meantime these amendments should be passed in order to give the working seamen the bene-i fits contained therein until such time as a complete revision of the act can take place.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know that it is necessary to add a great deal to the very clear exposition of this bill which has been presented by my colleague from Vancouver (Mr. Maclnnis). It is quite obvious that legislation passed in 1854, as was the present Canada Shipping Act, is entirely obsolete. I believe the minister has admitted that, so it is not necessary to stress the point.
In the old.act there is a definition of coastal trade, but at the present time a trade has developed between the ports -of Montreal and Vancouver which is commonly known in shipping circles as intercoastal trade. So far as I can learn there is absolutely no definition in the act as to what intercoastal trade really means. Under the old act and in the old days there was a provision by which a seaman in case of discharge might be taken back to his home port, but there is no provision at the present time for that kind of repatriation in the case of this intercoastal trade. A man may ship at Montreal and be discharged at Vancouver and then have to find his way home as best he can. It is absolutely ridiculous that such should be the case, because Vancouver, as we all know, is farther away from Montreal than are many foreign ports; it just happens that both ports are in Canada. In a number of instances the city of Vancouver has forced the shipping companies to send men home overland. There should be a definite safeguard with regard to a matter of this kind.
When the original act was drawn up in 1854 there was still a good deal of despotism at sea. I recognize that there must be discipline on board a ship and that the captain must have powers which are not ordinarily granted to an employer on land, but at the same time very frequent complaints are made of the arbitrary action of certain sea captains. Some of the officers who have been brought up in the old sailing ships imagine they are still back in that dajr and have not changed their attitude towards their men.
I believe that some points not mentioned in this bill will have to be taken up in the near future. For example, there is the fining of men for delinquencies of various kinds. The penalties are often excessive and there is no easy method of appeal.
In many instances conditions on board ship are considerably better than is required by the laws as they now stand. Many captains are actuated by humane considerations and they see to it that their seamen are well looked after, but of course there are certain captains who do not care anything about

Canada Shipping Act
their men, and I suppose it is to such that the laws are designed primarily to apply. The men ought to have some safeguards other than they have at the present time.
With regard to hours, I know that on many ships there is a day off; Sunday as we all know is taken as a sort of sailor's holiday. He is allowed that time to himself to clean up, wash his .clothes and so on, so that there is often not the ordinary routine on that one day of the week. On the other hand, however, the hours for certain classes of seamen are still long. Officers, engineers and firemen work four hours on and eight hours off; sailors, except the wheelmen, work four hours on and four off, making a twelve-hour day. Why not, as I understand is the case in United States ships, have an eight hour day for sailors? Why not, as in British ships, have extra pay for overtime? Under our act there is no provision for that sort of thing. Again and again the British North America Act has been put forward as an excuse for nonaction on the part of the federal government. Clearly this is a case for action on the part of the federal government. Conditions at sea come directly under the purview of the federal government, and we ought to see to it that the eight-hour -day for sailors is adopted.
My colleague the hon. member for South Vancouver (Mr. Ma-olnnis) did not dwell upon section 935, which would prohibit coastal trade from ships not registered in Canada. It may be that, as he said, such a provision is ultra vires of parliament and we may have to wait for the passing of the statute of Westminster. But I would point out the abuses that exist under the act as it stands to-day. Several years ago I cited a case in which Chinese sailors were employed in the Besco ships bringing coal from Sydney to Montreal-ordinary coastal work. It was said that they were employed in bond, and at that time we made strong protest against that kind of traffic. The following year, for some reason best known to that company, the Besco ships were registered in England and operated by an English company. We were then told, when we brought up this question of Chinese sailors, that the dominion government could not do anything about the matter because the boats were not of Canadian registry. Obviously an abuse of that kind ought not to be allowed to continue, and I hope when the minister is making his changes after the statute of Westminster comes into effect, he will see to it that the coastal trade 2211C-lBOi
is carried on only by ships of Canadian registry.
Trob&bly these are the only points that need special emphasis at this time. I quite recognize the fact that the amendments which are offered in this bill do not go far enough; there are scores of amendments not provided for by the bill but which ought to be introduced; in fact, the whole act needs overhauling from stem to stern. You cannot do much with it; you cannot patch it up to make it really seaworthy. These are only some of the outstanding evils, provisions for the removal of which might keep the old ship afloat for another twelve months until the minister can see his way clear to bring about a thorough revision of the act.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. J. COWAN (Port Anthur-Thunder Bay):
speechtext:
I have not had time to consider carefully all the amendments contained in the bill now before the house, which seeks to amend the Canada Shipping Aict. I desire, however, to discuss for a few minutes section 3 of the proposed bill, which seeks to amend section 935 of the original Canada Shipping Act. Perhaps it is because .this act was passed so many years ago that it does not now fulfil the requirements of operators and owners of Canadian shipping. It has been said that the whole act will be amended very shortly. I think it is wise at this time to state objections to the act as it exists at present, so that when the amendments are brought before the house, the government charged with the responsibility of amending the act will have these features in view.
Let me state a case which I think demands attention. Reports last week indicated that there were shipped out of the ports of Pbrt Arthur and Fort William 2,030,000 bushels of wheat for shipment down the St. Lawrence. This is Canadian wheat grown in Canada by Canadian farmers, and it may surprise hon. members to know that the total quantity of 2,000,000 bushels was shipped in United States bottoms. The other side of the picture is this, that in the ports of Port Arthur and Fort William there were standing idle that week fifteen Canadian bottoms with no cargoes. The space was there: the operators were willing to have their boats chartered, but all this wheat was shipped in United States bottoms. Such a situation ought not be tolerated.
Why not?

The matter
would be different if we did toot have the Canadian bottoms, but they were there, ready
Canada Shipping Act

for -cargoes. What happens is this: under our coastal laws we have not the same consideration as -the United States gives to their shipping interests. The United States law may be stated simply in these words:
No merchandise shall he transported by water under penalty of forfeiture thereof from one port of the United States to another port of the United States, either directly or via a foreign port, or for any part of the voyage, in any other vessel than a vessel of the United States.
Our shipping interests simply say: We desire to be put upon an equal footing with the shipping interests in the United States. Our law is such that a caigo of Canadian wheat may be shipped from the Canadian head of the lakes to Montreal in a United States boat provided that it first touches at the porit of Buffalo or any other United States port, is there unloaded into another United States boat and taken down the St. Lawrence river. I think I can say without fe-ar of contradiction that this is only a subterfuge whereby a United States boat can call at Port Arthur, take on a cargo of Canadian wheat, go to Buffalo and either unload it into an elevator or reload it into a canal-sized boat owned again by United States interests so tha-t i-t may be taken from Buffalo down to Montreal. Such a situation would not be tolerated so far as shipping of United States grain in Canadian bottoms from Duluth to Buffalo or other United States ports is concerned.
The law should also be amended in this regard: In the United States no foreigner may own any share in a boat if it is going to operate under their laws. In Canada such is not the case. At the present time, United States citizens can form a Canadian company and operate a boat or bring it in from the United States at a low valuation. This, I may say, has been done frequently. The Eastern Steamships Company, for instance, has established a head office at Port Colborne, where they keep a skeleton staff or the nucleus of an office, their real head office being in Buffalo. That is done simply to evade the Canadian regulations. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that our Canadian boat owners should be put on a parity with those of the United States. I suggest in all earnestness that this should be considered when the coastal laws are amended, and that such provision be made as well, make it not enough just to maintain a skeleton office in this country. The boats should be owned and operated by Canadian captains and Canadian seamen. I do not think at this stage I need labour the point, in view of the statement of the Prime Minister

a day or two ago that, when enabling legislation goes through, this country will have complete control of its shipping laws. I hope that at that time these [DOT] suggestions will be taken into consideration and the law amended accordingly.

As a representative of the western grain growers I take exception to the suggestion of the hon. member for Port Arthur-Thunder Bay (Mr. Cowan) that our grain should be shipped only in Canadian-owned boats. We farmers of the west claim the right to ship our grain by the cheapest boat we can get. We must reduce expenses at every possible turn in order to compete on the world market. It is no argument to say that because the United States discriminates against her farmers and delivers them into the hands of her shipping interests, therefore we should do the same. This government has no right to say to the western farmer: You must ship your grain by a Canadian boat even though it charges you more than an American boat. We claim the right to ship by the cheapest boat, and we will stand by that position.

That
argument -would be all right if my hon. friend allowed it to apply in the case of the elevators, instead of saying to the elevators: You will ship the grain just as we tell you.
Would the hon. gentleman explain just what he means?

If my hon. friend d-oes not understand what I -mean, I have not time to explain now. I want to say a word on our coastal laws. The trouble is that when the federal government-, in order to meet the situation to which the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) thas referred, abrogated our coastal laws so that Americans -could in times of stress come in and take Canadian grain, American shipowners deliberately violated the privilege granted the-m, and instead of simply bringing the grain down and storing in a Canadian port as they were -privileged to do, they unloaded it at a Canadian port and immediately returned to the head of ithe lakes for another cargo, in contravention of the conditions under which the -coastal laws were suspended. The result was that- our Canadian seamen sat idle last fall and the fall before, when the abrogation was made, with only g-ood intentions on the part -of the Canadian government. We repeatedly called the attention of the government to the situation, even giving the names of the American ships violating the law, but no action was taken. I trust, therefore, that this year the minister in charge of

The Budget-Mr. Beaubien
this department, a member on this side of the house, will 'be more careful of the interests of Canadian seamen than were hon. members opposite in the past.
Just in passing I would point out that whenever one does plead the cause of a Canadian workman my hon. friend from Weytourn is about the first man to get up on his feet and knock the proposal. If the Canada Shipping Act cannot now be revised, at the latest there should be a full revision nest year, including the amendments proposed here. There is not one interest on the Canadian side but is anxious for such a revision, and pending that revision I trust that the minister will see that the abrogation of the present coastal law shall be strictly observed and not violated as it has been in the past against the interests of our Canadian seamen.
As it is almost nine o'clock, Mr. Speaker, and I cannot finish my remarks 'before the hour for private bills expires, perhaps you would call it nine o'clock.
The minister may continue his remarks the next time this matter comes before the house.

I have listened with much interest to the remarks made by hon. members on this question, but I do not think the time is opportune to accept the principle of the bill sponsored by my hon. friend for Vancouver South (Mr. Maclnnis). As was stated the other day when my estimates were before the house, the intention of the government is, when we have full power, as we shall have in the very near future, to .make a complete revision of the Canada Shipping Act. We admit (that the act as it stands to-day should in .certain important particulars be amended for the protection of Canadian shipping interests and Canadian mariners. There is no doubt about that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In rising to make a few observations in the present debate, I intend to follow my usual practice and to be brief in anything that I
have to say. May I be permitted first to congratulate the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) for the very fine address which he gave yesterday in reply to the budget speech delivered by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett). In my experience in this house in the last ten years I do not think I have ever heard a reply to a budget speech more ably or more fairly presented.
I hope I shall be pardoned if I do not follow the remarks of my hon. friend from Stanstead (Mr. Hackett), who took his seat just before six o'clock, except to the extent of a few general Observations. It ill becomes any member of this house, no matter on which side of politics he belongs, especially at this time when the Canadian National Railway is facing a serious situation, as is practically every other business organization throughout the dominion, to try to lower the national railway in the estimation of the public. I have not the quotation before me, but I understand that in 1912 or 1913 the present Prime Minister referred to an hon. member of this house as the gramophone of the Mackenzie and Mann interests. May I be permitted, Mr. Speaker, to say I am inclined to believe that the hon. member for Stanstead, if one may judge by his attack this afternoon on the Canadian National Railways, is the gramophone of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I do not make that statement in criticism of the Canadian Pacific Railway, one of the finest organizations of its kind and one which is rendering a service to this country of which everybody should be proud. I repeat however that no man has a right to attack the Canadian National Railways to the extent they were attacked this afternoon, and no one has a right to create a false impression throughout the country concerning those railways. The remarks of my hon. friend from Stanstead reminded me of an eminent lawyer trying to boost his corporation by knocking another. No commercial traveller ever sold an article by knocking the article of a competitor; it is not good business. My hon. friend also referred to the swimming pool in the Chateau Laurier and wanted to know to what use the pool could be put. I am informed-and if my information is not accurate I wish to be corrected -that the right hon. the Prime Minister uses that swimming pool almost every day. Through the use of the pool he keeps himself fit. A man who has to do the work the Prime Minister does, a man trying to run

speechtext:
The hon. member for
Stanstead this afternoon attempted to criticize the efficiency of the Canadian National Railways. I fear no contradiction when I state that no railway in the world is giving more efficient service than the Canadian National Railways are giving to the Canadian people. The Canadian people are proud of the system, and the speech by my hon. friend this afternoon will not change their view in that .respect. In order to prove that the Canadian National Railways are considered by the 'Canadian people to be an exceptionally fine institution I refer hon. members to a speech .delivered on March 8, 1928 by the present (Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie). In that speech my hon. friend from Stanstead will find all the information he wishes regarding the Canadian National Railways.
I intend now to deal as briefly as possible with the budget. First I shall attempt to discuss the stamp tax on cheques, followed by some observations on the increase of the sales tax, the restoration of the tax on tea, the increased tariffs, amendments to the income tax, and the five cent speech of the right hon. the Prime Minister.
Before I go on with those remarks, however, may I tell the house at least a part of what I told my electors during the election campaign. I told them that if the right hon. gentleman-at that time I called him Mr. Bennett-became Prime Minister there would be several millionaires in his cabinet from whom the poorer people could not expect much sympathy. I do not know how many millionaires there are in the present cabinet. However, it makes no difference to me what the number is, because I can go back to my electors at the close of this session and say to them that even if there are not as many millionaires in the cabinet

as I had prophesied, the first budget presented at a regular session by the present Prime Minister of Canada is a rich man's budget, and none but the rich will receive any benefit from it.
During the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne the Prime Minister accused hon. members on this side of the house of exaggerating conditions in western Canada. He chastized us very severely. He went to the extent of telling us that we had produced $1,900,000,000 wealth in the last three years, that tens of thousands of farmers had money in the bank, that we had a great many automobiles, and that we paid a large sum of money by way of tax on gasoline. Those are true statements, Mr. Speaker. We did produce about $1,900,000,000 in wealth in the years mentioned. But where did that wealth go? Some of it went to the railroads, some of it to our institutions, and by the time we had finished producing it there was nothing left for us-nothing. It is a fact that a considerable sum was paid by way of gasoline tax, but who spent it? The tourists spent a great deal of it, but people in the cities spent most of it. Who own the automobiles in western Canada? Does the Prime Minister want to deprive the poor farmer of his "tin Lizzie?" Does he want him to keep his family at home and give them no enjoyment of any description? The statements made by the Prime Minister are true, Mr. Speaker; I am not denying them. I do however object to the information that he has broadcast throughout Canada in an attempt to create the impression that the farmer who is trying to get relief of some kind is wealthy and does not need relief.
In the same speech, and the next breath, the Prime Minister asked: What is the cause of the great depression? If there is a great depression hon. members on this side of the house simply place the situation before the government by telling them exact conditions. The Prime Minister admits there is a great depression. By providing in his budget speech for five cents per bushel on western wheat he has admitted that there is a depression. Tf there is any exaggeration of the economic condition of the western farmer, it can be traced to the inference broadcast by the Prime Minister in his speech of April 21. The truth is that conditions in western Canada are bad. The Prime Minister knows that, and if he does not it is because he has not tried to acquaint himself with the facts. I am afraid if conditions do not soon improve in western Canada the results will be disastrous.

The Budget-Mr. Beaubien
In my speech delivered in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne I said that prosperity would come to Canada just as soon as and no sooner than the agricultural industry was put on a paying basis. Nobody can successfully deny that statement. Neither the Prime Minister nor any other minister can deny it. Prosperity will come to Canada when the farming industry is put on a basis of prosperity whereby after working the whole year the farmers can have something left. I said, and I repeat, that there is only one way to bring that condition about. The Prime Minister admits, as I think every man who has made a study of world conditions in regard to the sale of cereals and other farm products will admit, that we must lower the cost of production. We cannot expect much higher prices for our products, so what is there for us to do? Are we to stop producing, or are we to try to reduce our costs of production in order to compete in the world markets? I claim that we must reduce our costs of production. But how are we to do that under a government which is imposing tax after tax on the people least able to bear the burden, and at the same time relieving those best able to bear it? How can we reduce our costs of production when this government is running wild with tariff increases? The Prime Minister is fond of having concrete examples put before him, and in a few moments I am going to give some examples of how the tariff works.
Now let me deal for a moment with the stamp tax on cheques under $10. A friend of mine shipped a five gallon can of cream the other day to Eaton's in Winnipeg. I will admit it was not No. 1 cream, but for that five gallon can he received $1.13. As soon as this stamp tax comes into force what will be done by Eaton's, by the dairies and the other milk purchasers? They will charge the farmers the two cents they have to put on the cheque, and on that five gallon can of cream, which netted my friend $1.13, that would amount almost to a two per cent tax. I hope my constituents will remember that I told them they could not expect anything else from a rich cabinet.
Then let us go on to the sales tax, which is being increased from one per cent to four per cent, while many commodities previously exempted are now to be subject to tax. More commodities which go into the cost of living and which are absolutely necessary will be taxed four per cent instead of one per cent, and this at a time when the poor people can hardly earn enough to support
their families. I am sorry the Minister of Justice is not in the house. The hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth quoted him yesterday in regard to the Canadian National Railways, and I should like to quote him in regard to the sales tax. In 1929 the late Mr. Robb reduced the sales tax from three per cent to two per cent, and the Minister of Justice, then sitting on this side of the house, had something to say in regard to that proposal. I find in Hansard for March 7, 1929, the following:
When it comes down to the ordinary, everyday people of Canada, all he has to say to them is this: I have taken one per cent off the sales tax. That is some relief. The sales tax last year at three per cent yielded sixty million dollars. Next year at two per cent the yield will be twenty million dollars less. But why maintain this war tax which is so burdensome upon the backs of the poorer people of the dominion?
The minister almost had crocodile tears in his eyes. He went on to say:
Do the people know even yet that they have to pay two per cent on their wearing apparel, one per cent on their boots and shoes, and two per cent on practically everything that goes into the ordinary household?
If this statement held good at that time, Mr. Speaker, it holds good to-day when the poor people are much less able to pay the sales tax than they were in 1929. Yet the tax is increased from one per cent to four per cent.
Then we come to the restoration of the tax on tea. Now that the price of liquor is so thigh we have to drink itea, butt what will happen? As soon as this tax is put -back I am afraid the people will have to go back to liquor. Why not make everything the people must have as cheap as possible? Why put on this tax while relieving the rich man of the income tax? It is not logical; it is not common sense; it is not fair; it is not equitable.
Now we come to the tariff increases, which will take a tremendous toll from the Canadian people. I am not a free trader, as the word is usually understood; I know it is impossible to have free trade at the present time, but I do not think we should go in for higher and higher protection for our industries. Our industries are controlled by human beings. They are taking advantage of the tariff to the fullest extent; they always have done so and always will do so. In that connection I have two or three concrete examples for the consideration of the Prime Minister. During the short session last September, when the Prime Min-
The Budget-Mr. Beaubien

ister was presenting to the house the proposed increases in the tariff, he said he had guarantees from the people who were getting the increased protection that they would not increase the prices of their goods. The Prime Minister placed on Hansard letter after letter from these different firms. What did we say on this side, and -whait do I say now? I say he cannot prevent these people from increasing the prices of their goods unless he is going to oversee every little detail of all these companies. How would the bon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) like to have the Prime Minister, or the auditors of the Department of Finance, looking through his books in order to find out whether or not he was charging too much for his goods?

Now I am going to give some further examples to the Prime Minister, and I hope he will do -me the courtesy of looking into these matters. I presented one case to the Minister of National Revenue last fall in regard to fruit, but I have heard nothing more about it. The government just -put on new duties whenever they feel like it; they go from oranges to potatoes and to radishes and increase the [DOT]tariff. Here is a concrete case of a price increase. J. W. Miller and Company, of Toronto, are manufacturers of equipment -for poultry farms. They do a large mail order business and publish annually illustrated informative catalogues. I have here a comparison of their catalogue prices of 1930 and 1931. The tariff was increased at the short session from 10 per cent to 25 per cent, an increase of 15 per cent. Now, there has been a substantial increase in the prices of the commodities sold by this concern-the commodities which are indispensable to the chicken-raising business and which the chicken-raiser must have if he is to put eggs on the market. And wh-ile these prices have gone up, the chicken-raiser is getting 5 cents a dozen in the west for his eggs. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have given a sufficient number of illustrations to show what the trend is. In other words, since the special session the prices of these commodities have gone up between 10 and 12 per cent. These articles the farmer must procure if he is to carry on business, and while their prices have gone up there has been a decline from about 22 cents to 5 cents a dozen in the price of eggs in the west. Is there any justice in such a condition of things? I repeat, notwithstanding what the hon. member for Lincoln may think, that these high tariffs will result in an increased cost of production. It cannot be otherwise. Let me give you an illustration from my own experience. At Easter the Prime Minister was kind enough to give us a long holiday and I thought I would go home and see what my constituents had to say in regard to what this government has done. I should hate to tell you, sir, what they told me to come here and say, because it would be unparliamentary. However, being a farmer, I happened to be in need of a smutcleaning machine. For your benefit, Mr. Deputy Speaker, although I believe you were brought up on a farm yourself, I may describe the smut-cleaning machine. Every year we have to pass our grain through a formalin solution in order to safeguard it from smut. This is a technical term which may not be familiar to the house. When the grain matures the ear may turn into a black

The Budget-Mr. Beaubien
powder and you have no grain. Consequently we have to put the grain through this solution every year, and it is one of the most essential of our farming operations. Now, I went to my dealer to buy one of these smuLeleaning machines and I asked him what he wanted for it. He gave me both his 1930 and 1931 price lists. In 1980 an 18 inch smut machine with perforated bottom and extra long carriers cost, f.o.b. Winnipeg, $24; Saskatoon, $26; and Edmonton, $27. In 1931 the price of that very same machine had increased. Mind you, they did not go to the trouble of printing a new price list; they simply took a little piece of yellow paper with the new prices printed on it, and pasted that slip over the old prices. Apparently they did not want to go to the expense of printing a new list. In 1931 the price of that 18 inch smut machine, f.o.b., was $28 in Winnipeg; $30 in Saskatoon; and $31 m Edmonton. Perhaps I had better give the name of the firm: it is The Hart-Emerson Co., Ltd., of Winnipeg, Saskatoon and Edmonton. They make these machines. Well, I asked my dealer the reason for the increase in price, but he said he did not know. What was the result so far as trade was concerned? Why, I simply refused to buy the machine. Instead, I went home, took out my old machine and fixed it up the best way I could. I came back to Ottawa and went into the tariff in order to find out just what the situation was. I found that smut machines are dutiable under tariff item 409, subitem (f), and the duty in force prior to the special session of last September was: British preferential, free; intermediate, 10 per cent; general tariff, 10 per cent. At the September session the Canada first policy was carried into effect. That is now a famous slogan- Canada first. An hon. gentleman says it means, "Soak the Canadian people." I think he is right-soak them first and others afterwards. The Prime Minister increased this duty, making the rates: British preferential, free; intermediate, 15 per cent; general tariff, 25 per cent. Now, the British preference does not figure here at all; the only tariff that figures in this is the general tariff, and that tariff was increased 15 per cent. My hon. friend from St. Boniface (Mr. Howden) tells me-and I think he is right-that 75 per cent of durum wheat, of which we grow a great deal in the west, is subject to smut and must be treated all the time. Now, what was the increase in the tariff on the article so greatly needed in this regard? The increase, f.o.b. Winnipeg, was 16 per cent; Saskatoon, 15
per cent; and Edmonton, 14 per cent. Remember, Mr. ^Speaker, that the British preference does not apply here. The only tariff which would apply is the general tariff, and that was increased by 15 per cent. The price of the machine was increased by 15 per cent, which proves beyond question that my contention is correct. I can pass this list to any hon. member to show that the price of the machine was increased by the exact amount of the increase in the tariff. These tariff changes increased the price of the commodities which the farmer needs in order to carry on his operations.
I repeat, and I hope that the Prime Minister will read my remarks, that prosperity will come to Canada just as soon as and no sooner than the agricultural industry is put on a paying basis. Every action of this government, as shown by this present budget and the results of the last session, has aggravated the situation and increased the cost of production to the farmer.
For a few minutes I would like to discuss the wheat situation and the five cent speech of the Prime Minister. We heard a good deal about the five cent speech of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) during the last campaign, but we now have another hon. gentleman in this house who comes within the same category. I do not know very much about this five cent bounty on freight rates on export wheat, and I have not been alble to find any other hon. member who does. I have asked every hon. member with whom I have come in contact- except you, Mr. Speaker, and I am sorry I did not go to you; perhaps if I had I would have obtained the information I desired. No one has been able to give me any explanation as to how it is going to be applied. I do not know how the government intends to get it back to the farmer. I suppose the Prime Minister will be able to give the house some explanation. Why not put a five cent bonus on barley? The province of Manitoba in 1929 produced 28,565,000 bushels of wheat, and in 1930, 45,278,000 bushels. The barley production in 1929 amounted to 36,518,000, and in 1930, 49,974,000 bushels. We produced more barley than wheat. What relief is offered to the man who has sown barley this year and who has not sown any wheat? Wheat cannot be sown every year; the crops must be rotated.
If the Prime Minister wants to give relief to the farmer-and I suppose that is what he intends to do-I hope he is not trying to convert him to his system of protection by giving him this five cent bounty on freight. If the
The Bridget-Mr. Beaubien

Prime Minister is trying to give relief to the farmer, this five cent piece is wholly inadequate, and he knows it. If he desires to give relief to western Canada, let him give the farmer something tangible, let him give to the farmer as much as he is giving to the manufacturers.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether I may be considered as fortunate or unfortunate in following the hon. member who has just resumed his seat (Mr. Beaubien). At the outset I desire to express my gratification for the budget brought down by our esteemed leader (Mr. Bennett). It was a comprehensive and courageous budget-comprehensive because it entered into every detail of the economic life of Canada, and courageous because it takes courage to impose taxation upon a people. The taxation was necessary because we were in dire straits; we are going to see if we cannot balance our budget during the coming year.
I do not intend to take up very much of the time of the house in discussing the subject matter of the budget, as I have not heard any arguments advanced from the other side of the house which call for refutation. On the other hand, I have heard some magnificent arguments by the hon. members for East Essex (Mr. Morand) and Cumberland (Mr. Smith). The hon. member for Cumberland has shown how this budget will give great relief to the iron and steel industry. He speaks with authority, as he is familiar with the conditions which exist in that part of the country. The hon. member for East Essex gave as an illustration how each automobile built in Canada meant $450 or the equivalent

The Budget-Mr. Dickie
of three months' work to workmen engaged in its manufacture. We should build our own automobiles in Canada; we are ten years behind with this budget program in this country, and there is no reason why we cannot build automobiles here? If we had built in Canada automobiles equal to the number that wo imported in 1929 from the United States, we would have had 11,000 workingmen employed at good wages doing that work and that would have meant an additional population of 50,000 in this country.
This budget is an additional step to stem the outflow of capital from this country to the United States. It will stem the tide of imports and help to keep our money here, and if we keep our money here, we shall be doing the best that can be done under the present conditions. Surely no hon member would say that we should carry on as we did in 1926 and 1927, those halcyon years when there was a balance of trade of $400,000,000 against us in favour of the United States. Those people were laughing at us; they called us gentlemen and fine people, but they wondered at our simplicity in permitting such a condition of affairs to exist. They were accepting our raw material, welcoming it, but we could not get them to accept from Canada anything into which Canadian labour entered. Finally it was decided that a tariff would have to be imposed, and Mr. Dunning, more for political purposes than anything else, had a tariff regulation enacted at that time. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has said-and he is living up to his promises - that he is going to stem the tide of imports and to make this Canada of ours a self-supporting country. There is no reason why we cannot bring that about. We can keep our money here; we can keep our people here, and now that we have put a stop to immigration from Europe, there is no reason why we should not have more stable conditions in this country when we once more get on our feet. When that time comes we can pass social legislation for the benefit of our wage earners to give them the treatment which we cannot accord to them at the present time.
I did not intend to say anything with respect to the budget, because it has been so ably dealt with by others who have already spoken. My reason for addressing the house to-night is that we have grievances in British Columbia and although we have not been heard crying out, we have had our backs against the wall. We have taken our medicine standing up, but we in that province still have many problems
confronting us. It is my hope to-night that what I say may induce the government to grant us a little more relief than has been accorded in the past in order that we may come through the trying times through which we are at present passing.
Last season we had a magnificent catch of fish in British Columbian waters. Our individual fishermen made good money but our canners are on the verge of bankruptcy. One canning company lost over a million dollars last year, for the simple reason that they could not sell their pack in the markets of Europe. They had built up in France quite a market for our red salmon when Russian representatives told the French people that no matter at what price Canadian canners put their salmon on the market, the Russians would let them have theirs at fifty cents a case cheaper. In regard to this I am speaking of something that I know is absolutely the case. Russian salmon entered into Great Britain and the markets of continental Europe and we were unable to sell our salmon at prices that would be profitable to the British Columbia canners.
We have a metalliferous province, if I may put it in that way, and with copper at the present time at eight cents a pound, lead at four cents, zinc at about the same price, and silver very low, our mining men are in despair and we would like to see something done for them.
As regards lumber, we have the same story to tell. We have a wonderful lumber industry in British Columbia. We ship our lumber to Great Britain, but we now find that the British market is supplied from Russian sources. We have lost large orders there and the lumbermen of British Columbia hardly know what to do at the present time, due to the great Russian menace. We do not hlame any government for the troubles that I have mentioned in these three industries; they are the result of world-wide conditions. We cannot help what that soulless country, Russia, does at this time, but still we are handicapped to a great extent by their lumber, fish, and also wheat; because we look to the prairie provinces to buy much of our produce from British Columbia and the price of wheat being forced down by the wheat from Argentina and Russia, the people of the prairie provinces are unaible to purchase as they used to do from British Columbia producers.
But there is something that I think can be done with respect to the coal situation. We have coal mines in British Columbia, and

Many of the men employed in the mines on Vancouver island are British miners; they have their little homes there, and the hardships which they are enduring at present are more than they should be expected to bear. They are willing to work. During the war, when we were having all sorts of trouble with the foreign mining element in Brule and other places to the east, our miners stuck to their work, never asked for a cent extra pay, and came through clean and creditable to British Columbia. We want to see something done for these men.
The Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleiau) has very graciously given us a hydrographic 
steamer to work on the Pacific coast. Although it was represented that fuel oil had to be used on that steamer, I am proud to say that the minister supported us nobly and said that it mudt burn coal. That, of course, is simiply a gesture, but it gives a little heart, to the coal miners of British Columbia. We have an immense hotel being erected at a cost of 18,000,000. We made representations at Ottawa to have coal burned in that hotel, but Sir Henry Thornton, or those under him, said that this was an impossibility; they would not aocede to our request. They said that it would cost $5,000 additional to burn coal over what it would cost to bum oil. We still continued our efforts; we told them that those figures were absurd; but even if such were the case, the ooal would be brought from Nanaimo, which is a very good customer of the city of Vancouver. We did not cease our efforts in the matter, and just the other day we were informed by the Minister of Bail-ways and Canals (Mr. Manion) that coal will be burned in the great furnaces of that hotel. There is no reason why this should not have been done, and I am glad indeed that pressure was brought to bear to that end. There was some reason why the management of the railway changed their ideas with respect to the fuel they would burn in that hotel. It will mean work for some of the miners, because it is a large hotel and I am sure they will ge't along just as well with ooal as with fuel oil. We instanced the ease of the Empress hotel at Victoria, as pretty a hotel as there is in the world. They have been burning coal and are well satisfied with it, and we saw no reason why the Canadian National should not do the same in a hotel belonging to the people of this country. It would mean giving a little work to the miners of this country, instead of sending the money out of Canada to California for fuel oil.
Let me give a few figures to show the inroads fuel oil has made on the coal industry in Canada. In 1926 we produced in British Columbia 42,000,000 gallons of fuel oil from crude oil refined and admitted free of duty, and in 1930, 130,000,000 gallons. We imported in the same years fuel oil to the amount of 62,0000,000 gallons and 30,000,000 gallons respectively. That oil all came in from California. The reason why the fuel importations fell off from 62,000,000 to 30,000,000 between 1926 and 1930 was due to the fact that the dominion government imposed a. duty of half a cent a gallon on fuel oil. The crude oil which is refined in British Columbia and from which fuel oil is produced, and

The Budget-Mr. Dickie
gasoline and other gaseous products, leaves fuel oil as the residue, and it is this oil coming in from California with which we have to compete in British Columbia. Last year we bought from the United States 130,000,000 gallons of that fuel oil. That would represent about $5,000,000 or $6,000,000, which went to enrich the oil people of California. We believe that the people of British Columbia will be quite willing to burn coal if we can put the question properly before them. We are told by the coal people that a regional duty in the way of an excise tax of one cent or one and a half cents a gallon would give employment to between 500 and 1,000 men in our coal mines at Nanaimo, Cumberland and Ladysmith, nice little towns where the miners are now walking around hollow-eyed looking for work. Such a duty would mean that these men would get work and would be able to live on in the little homes where they hope to spend the rest of their days. This would be a regional tariff not affecting any other part of Canada. The people of Vancouver city, who are the greatest consumers of fuel oil, I feel sure would not object any too strongly to a tax of that kind. Of course, there would have to be exemptions with respect to some parts of the lumber industry and with respect to the oceanic steamers plying from the port of Vancouver. They would have to receive a rebate of that one cent or one and a half cents a gallon on the fuel oil imported. Such a step would be of incalculable benefit to the coal industry of British Columbia.
The Prime Minister has proposed in the budget to give a bonus of 25 cents a ton on coal used for fuel purposes, for ship's stores or for export. We appreciate that bonus. It will do some good, but it will not accomplish what we wish to accomplish. I know of no reason why we should send out of this country four or five or six million dollars to enrich the people of California, and at the same time have our coal miners working only part time and sometimes not working at all. Let us keep that four or five or six million dollars in British Columbia and put our own people to work, and then we will have contented communities, things will go on very much better, the money will remain in our country and each of us may get a chance at it. There may be lions in the path; it may be impossible to carry this out, but I am going to expend all the power I have in trying to induce the government to grant further relief to the coal mining industry of British Columbia.
I have been a little amused iby some of the statements that have been made on the other side of the house with respect to our worthy and esteemed leader. One matter that has been frequently brought up by hon. members opposite is that the Prime Minister said, according to them, that immediately he came into power he would end unemployment. Whether he said that he would immediately end unemployment when he .came into power, or that he would immediately take action to end it, I do not know, but the question is so simple that I am amazed that hon. members opposite bring it up time and time again. No child on the street would expect the Prime Minister to end unemployment immediately. He meant doubtless that he would take immediate steps looking towards ending unemployment. This he has done, and when I hear hon. members opposite belittling the granting, of the $20,000,000 appropriated last September to help the unemployed in Canada I marvel at them, because that money provided work for a great many people, and the people are grateful for it.
Another matter of which hon. members opposite speak in a belittling way is the five cents a bushel bonus on wheat shipped from the prairies, which this budget grants. I know that five cents does not sound very impressive. I do not know just how this will be administered, but five cents a bushel on, say, 400,000,000 bushels, which we estimate will be the output of the prairies this year, amounts to $20,000,000, which the people throughout the rest of Canada are ready to pay in order to try to do something to help that badly harassed industry of agriculture in the prairie provinces. It is not becoming of hon. members opposite to 'belittle such assistance.
I am sure, also, that the people of Canada will be willing to pay the taxes which the Prime Minister proposes in this budget in order to stem the influx of imports into this country, because such action will result in keeping the money in this country and provide work for our own people. The people believe that the Prime Minister is doing the best that can be done. This is a time to perplex the souls of men, but I am sure that the people believe that the Prime Minister is giving of his best to bring Canada once more back on an even keel, and when that time arrives I hope that we shall not be wafted by indulgent breezes away again from the shores of sanity by trying to keep up with the Jones's and spending our money lavishly, laying nothing aside for the grey days of lean years which must inevitably recur in all countries. If our
Questions

people in many districts of British Columbia that I know of had only lived a little more carefully, there would not 'be the dire distress that there is to-day. This keeping up with the Jones's is all right, but it does not work out when the grey days come, and if nothing has been learnt from these dark days but the lesson of thrift and the making of provision for a rainy day, something worth while will come out of it all.
